cards.explanation: The answer is that the prayer asks the LORD to remember what has happened to them. It opens with "Remember, O LORD, what has happened to us." Then it adds, "Look and see our disgrace!" (Lamentations 5:1). No warm-up, no small talk, just straight to Him. It's like a text that says "call me" and nothing else, friends.

The answer is True. The prayer says, "Our inheritance has been turned over to strangers, our houses to foreigners." Inheritance means the land handed down in a family. Picture coming home and finding somebody else's name on the mailbox. Ouch.

The answer is their wood. The prayer says, "We must buy the water we drink; our wood comes at a price." Water AND wood, both with a price tag. Wood is what you burn to keep warm and cook. In my bakery, the oven's the one thing I never want to be short on.

The answer is Egypt and Assyria. The prayer says, "We submitted to Egypt and Assyria to get enough bread." Egypt and Assyria were two other nations. Bread was the reason the prayer gives. Getting enough of it is what the line is about.

The blanks are "fathers" and "punishment." The prayer says, "Our fathers sinned and are no more, but we bear their punishment." It's a heavy line, and I won't pretend otherwise. The ones who sinned are gone now, and the ones left are the ones talking to the LORD. The prayer says it plainly, with no dressing it up, friends. They're carrying it, and they say so to the LORD.

The answer is slaves. The prayer says, "Slaves rule over us…" It's describing how upside down things have gotten. Those who rule now are the ones you'd never expect. That's one more thing it hands to the LORD.

The answer is False. The verse says, "there is no one to deliver us from their hands." It says nothing about someone being on the way. It's a hard thing to say, friends, and the prayer says it anyway.

The answer is hunger. The verse says, "Our skin is as hot as an oven with fever from our hunger." The fever is the picture, and hunger is the cause the prayer names. It's another heavy line, so I'll just say that once.

The answer is False. The prayer says "elders receive no respect." Elders, the older leaders, aren't getting any. It's one more piece of how things have turned over, and it goes right alongside "Princes have been hung up by their hands…"

The answer is that they're toiling at millstones. The prayer says, "Young men toil at millstones…" A millstone is a heavy stone used for grinding grain. It's hard work, and I'd wobble just looking at it. The next line even gives the boys a load to carry.

The answer is mourning. The prayer says, "Joy has left our hearts; our dancing has turned to mourning." Dancing is joy you can see, and here it's gone to mourning. I think that line is one of the saddest in the prayer. It takes the lively thing and flips it.

The answer is True. The prayer says, "Woe to us, for we have sinned!" Earlier it said, "Our fathers sinned and are no more…" (Lamentations 5:7). Now "we" owns it too. It's honest, and it keeps right on praying.

The answer is that Mount Zion lies desolate. The prayer says, "…Mount Zion, which lies desolate, patrolled by foxes." Desolate means empty and left behind. The prayer says their eyes grow dim because of Mount Zion. I think that's the heart of their grief.

The answer is that He reigns forever and His throne endures. The prayer says, "You, O LORD, reign forever; Your throne endures from generation to generation." It says this out loud right after naming all that loss. That's a big turn in the prayer, friends.

The answer is True. The very next line asks, "Why have You forgotten us forever? Why have You forsaken us for so long?" Those are the prayer's own words and its own question. It holds "You, O LORD, reign forever…" and that aching question side by side, and it doesn't hide either one.

The answer is Himself. The prayer says, "Restore us to Yourself, O LORD, so we may return…" They aren't asking first for a place. They're asking to be brought back to Him. A big ask indeed, friends, and it comes from the heart.

The answer is False. The last line says, "…unless You have utterly rejected us and remain angry with us beyond measure." The fear is still out in the open when the prayer ends. I think it's honest, and they bring it to the LORD instead of keeping it quiet.
